extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and practitioners assessing §101 eligibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter is patent-eligible under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (with focus on Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B inventive-concept analysis). Intended to direct examiners how to identify and analyze additional claim elements and various considerations relevant to §101 determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that treats or prevents a disease or medical condition (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limitation is merely an intended use, field-of-use limitation, or does not require the substance actually be used by/on the patient (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient with eczema' or labeling a product as a 'pharmaceutical composition'), it is not an affirmative treatment/prophylaxis limitation and cannot integrate a judicial exception under the 'treatment or prophylaxis' consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity of treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment/prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular,' i.e., specifically identified so it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a claim reciting 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker medication to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype' (particular) vs 'administering a suitable medication to a patient' (not particular). Examiners may also evaluate related considerations such as mere instructions to apply an exception, and field-of-use/technological environment when assessing particularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: More-than-nominal relationship to the judicial exception(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment/prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'treating a patient having blood glucose over 250 mg/dl with insulin' has a significant relationship to the correlation between high glucose and ketoacidosis; 'treating ... with aspirin' does not (nominal connection). Consider also the insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use/technological environment factors when assessing relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation must not be mere extra-solution activity or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed treatment/prophylaxis must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and must not be merely extra-solution activity (e.g., steps performed only to gather data) or a field-of-use restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: (a) administering vaccines to gather data for a mental analysis (extra-solution, not integrative) vs (c) vaccinating a second group according to the lowest-risk schedule determined by the analysis (integrative, applies the exception). Evaluate with insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use/technological environment considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B begins by identifying any and all additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should carry over additional-element identifications from Step 2A Prong Two and use them as the basis for the inventive-concept analysis. Claims must be analyzed individually (each claim may be treated differently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept cannot be the judicial exception itself
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept 'cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature (or natural phenomenon or abstract idea) itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept must be an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception that ensures the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception alone (Alice/Mayo precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional elements amount to significantly more both when considered individually and when considered as an ordered combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if no single element amounts to significantly more on its own, a non-conventional or non-generic arrangement of known conventional elements may provide an inventive concept (see BASCOM, CellzDirect). Courts require considering claim elements 'as a whole' and in ordered combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate §101 inventive-concept analysis with novelty/obviousness (§102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept is distinct from novelty and non-obviousness inquiries; lack of novelty under §102 or obviousness under §103 is not determinative of §101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not substitute §§102/103 or §112 inquiries for the §101 analysis. Evidence that an element is known in the art does not automatically mean it cannot be an inventive concept when combined unconventionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to the functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that purport to improve the functioning of the computer itself or any other technology/technical field can qualify as 'significantly more' in the §101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting such an improvement, the specification should provide sufficient technical detail to make the improvement apparent to a person of ordinary skill. The claim must reflect the disclosed improvement (though not necessarily by literal language like 'thereby increasing bandwidth'). Evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination' and avoid oversimplifying. See McRO (automation of animation tasks) and DDR (technological solution to technological problem) examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a particular machine (one understood in the art to have a specific structure and arranged in a particular way) can supply significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: arranging a Fourdrinier machine in a particular way to optimize speed and quality (Eibel Process Co.). Consider whether the machine arrangement is conventional or non-conventional in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed process that effects a transformation of a particular article to a different state or thing can amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded rubber products (Diehr). The transformation must be meaningful and tied to the claimed steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding specific non-conventional limitations that confine the claim to a particular useful application
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding limitations other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: BASCOM—non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content. The added limitations must be more than generic or high-level recitations of conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of an exception to a particular technological environment can amount to significantly more when it meaningfully ties the exception to that environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example positive: immunization step integrating data comparison into a specific immunizing process that lowers disease risk (Classen). Example negative: merely limiting an abstract idea to the commodities market (Bilski) or to petrochemical fields (Parker v. Flook). Evaluate whether the linkage meaningfully confines the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations found insufficient to supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of limitation-types that the courts have held are not enough to make a claim 'significantly more' than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities at a high level of generality; (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering (CyberSource); (iv) generally linking the exception to a technological environment or field-of-use without meaningful limitation (Bilski, Flook). These should not be treated as inventive concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere physicality or tangibility is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physical or tangible implementation of an exception is neither necessary nor sufficient to establish an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A computer is a tangible machine, but simply reciting a generic computer does not render an abstract idea patent-eligible (Alice). Conversely, intangible/non-physical additional elements can support eligibility if they constitute an improvement in a technological process (Enfish, McRO examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must support asserted technical improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant asserts that the invention improves conventional computer functioning or technology, the specification must contain sufficient technical explanation such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conclusory assertion of improvement in the specification is insufficient. The specification need not literally state the improvement phrase, but must describe details or a technical problem/solution that make the improvement apparent (compare McRO vs Affinity Labs). After finding disclosure of improvement, ensure the claim scope reflects that improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation and as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should review the entire disclosure, construe claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation, and evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid oversimplifying claims by ignoring specific claim requirements. Consider dependent claims separately — one claim in an application may be ineligible while another dependent claim may recite additional elements that amount to significantly more. Follow the MPEP flowchart (Step 2B leads to YES eligible (Pathway C) or NO ineligible → §101 rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-evaluate elements previously characterized as insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements identified previously as insignificant extra-solution activity (per MPEP §2106.05(g)) should be re-evaluated in Step 2B to determine whether they might be unconventional or more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A re-evaluation that finds unconventionality may change the earlier conclusion and indicate the element or combination contributes an inventive concept. Examiners should also evaluate whether additional elements are merely conventional activities appended at a high level of generality (MPEP §2106.05(d)).
